model.title: Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians Land Transfer Act of 2026

summary.lead: Official summary (Congressional Research Service, Reported to House):

blocks.text: Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians Land Transfer Act of 2026

This bill takes three parcels of specified federal land (approximately 847 acres) in San Diego County, California, into trust for the benefit of the Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians of the Barona Reservation, California. The land taken into trust shall be part of the Tribe's reservation.

One parcel (approximately 164 acres) is currently administered by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), and two parcels (approximately 683 acres) are currently administered by the Forest Service. Administrative jurisdiction over the Forest Service land must be transferred to the Department of the Interior.

Among other requirements, the bill requires the land taken into trust to remain subject to (1) existing liens, rights-of-way, reciprocal road rights-of-way agreements, licenses, leases, permits, special use permits, and easements; (2) continuing public access to the land, including roads and trails, as on the date of the bill's enactment; and (3) rights-of-way necessary for BLM and Forest Service employees to access the land for operational and emergency purposes (e.g., wildfire suppression).
The bill requires the Tribe to maintain the fuel break within two of the parcels in accordance with applicable Forest Service standards.
The bill prohibits gaming on the land taken into trust.

This bill would move about 847 acres of federal land in San Diego County, California, into trust for the Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians. Once in trust, the land becomes part of the Tribe's reservation. Of the total, about 164 acres are currently managed by the Bureau of Land Management, and about 683 acres are managed by the Forest Service. The bill requires the Forest Service land's administrative control to be transferred to the Department of the Interior.

The land will keep several existing arrangements. Current liens, rights-of-way, road agreements, licenses, leases, permits, special use permits, and easements will remain in place. Public access to the land, including roads and trails, will continue as it was on the date the bill is enacted. Federal employees will also keep the access rights they need for management and emergencies, such as fighting wildfires.
The Tribe must maintain the fuel break within two of the parcels according to applicable Forest Service standards.
Finally, the bill bans gaming on the land placed in trust.
